title: Raise to an Integer Power
statement:
Given a floating-point number x and an integer n, return x raised to the power n, that is x multiplied by itself n times. n can be zero or negative: x⁰ = 1 and x⁻ᵏ = 1 / xᵏ.

Do it yourself without Math.pow, ** or similar. n can be as large as about two billion in either direction, so multiplying one step at a time is too slow. Answers within a relative error of 10⁻⁵ are accepted.

examples.why: 1.5 · 1.5 · 1.5. Plain repeated multiplication is fine here; the next two examples are where it breaks.
A negative power is one over the positive power: 1 / 2³ = 1 / 8. Ignoring the sign gives 8.
About two billion multiplications is far too slow, so square instead: about 31 steps. In Java or C++ a 32-bit int cannot hold +2147483648, so writing n = −n here silently stays negative.

hints: x¹⁶ is (x⁸)², x⁸ is (x⁴)², and so on. How many multiplications does that take compared with 16?
For any n: xⁿ = (x^(n/2))² when n is even, and x · (x^((n−1)/2))² when n is odd. Each step halves n, so there are about log₂ n steps.
Handle a negative n first: replace x with 1 / x and n with −n. Then loop over the bits of n, squaring x each round and multiplying it into the answer when the current bit is 1.

explain.intuition:
Multiplying x into a running product n times is O(n): two billion steps for the biggest inputs. The trick is squaring. x² · x² = x⁴, x⁴ · x⁴ = x⁸, so each squaring doubles the exponent. Any n is a sum of powers of two (its binary digits), so xⁿ is the product of the matching squares. For n = 13 = 8 + 4 + 1, x¹³ = x⁸ · x⁴ · x¹. That takes about log₂ n ≈ 31 squarings instead of billions of multiplications.

Negative powers just flip x: x⁻ⁿ = (1/x)ⁿ. Here is the interview trap. In Java or C++, n is a 32-bit int whose range is −2³¹ to 2³¹ − 1. Negating −2³¹ gives +2³¹, which does not fit, so it wraps back to −2³¹ and the loop misbehaves. The fix there is to copy n into a 64-bit long before negating. JavaScript numbers hold 2³¹ exactly, so -n is safe, but bit operators like n >> 1 and n & 1 convert to 32-bit ints and break on 2³¹. Use Math.floor(n / 2) and n % 2 instead.
steps: While n > 0: if n is odd, multiply result by x. Then square x and halve n (rounding down).
pitfalls: Negating n = −2³¹ in a 32-bit int (Java, C++, C#). It overflows back to −2³¹. Widen to a 64-bit type first.
Using >> or & on n in JavaScript. They work on 32-bit ints, so 2147483648 >> 1 is −1073741824 and the loop never ends correctly.
Recursing as power(x, n/2) * power(x, n/2), calling it twice. That is back to O(n) work. Compute the half once and square it.

solutions.title: Recursive halving
solutions.idea: Compute x to the half power once, square it, and multiply in one extra x when n is odd.

solutions.title: Iterative fast exponentiation
solutions.idea: Walk the binary digits of n from the lowest. Square x each round and multiply it into the result when the current bit is 1.

followups: Compute xⁿ modulo a large prime for integer x. What changes, and why is this the core of RSA?
Use the same squaring idea to raise a 2 × 2 matrix to a power. What sequence does that compute in O(log n)?
x can be 0 and n negative. What should the function do, and how would you report it?
